lead: Two DFA states are equivalent when no input string can tell them apart. If a string is accepted from one state and rejected from the other, that string distinguishes the pair. The table-filling algorithm finds every distinguishable pair, round by round, starting from pairs with one final and one non-final state. The unmarked pairs then merge, giving a DFA with no redundant states. This matters because the minimal DFA is the cleanest machine for a regular language, and it is unique up to renaming. Tools that build scanners, pattern matchers and protocol checkers use this reduction to keep state tables small.
prereq: You need 1.3 for the extended transition function δ̂ and 1.2 for DFA notation; 1.6 gives the wider idea of equivalent machines.

blocks.text: Fix a DFA M = (Q, Σ, δ, q0, F). Q is the finite state set, Σ is the input alphabet, δ: Q × Σ → Q is the transition function, q0 is the start state, and F ⊆ Q is the set of final states. For a state p and a string w, δ̂(p, w) is the state reached from p after reading all of w. This is the extended transition function from 1.3.

Two states p and q are distinguishable if some string w ∈ Σ* sends exactly one of δ̂(p, w) and δ̂(q, w) into F. That w is a distinguishing string. If no such string exists, p and q are equivalent, written p ≡ q. Equivalently, p ≡ q iff for every w ∈ Σ*, δ̂(p, w) ∈ F ⇔ δ̂(q, w) ∈ F.

The empty string is a valid test: it separates p and q when one is final and the other is not. Longer strings test the future. The relation ≡ is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, so it splits Q into classes. States in one class accept exactly the same strings: for every w, either both end in F or neither does. Merging a class into one state therefore cannot change the language.
The table-filling algorithm uses a triangular table. Each unordered pair {p, q} with p ≠ q appears once. A mark means 'these two are distinguishable'.

items: Delete every state not reachable from q0 by any string.
Mark every pair with one final and one non-final state. These are distinguished by the empty string.
Repeat a full pass over all unmarked pairs. For pair (p, q) and each a ∈ Σ, look at (δ(p, a), δ(q, a)). If that pair is already marked, mark (p, q). A pass that adds no mark stops the algorithm.
After stopping, all unmarked pairs are equivalent. Merge them into classes.

blocks.text: Why it works: pass 0 handles distinguishing strings of length 0. If pass k−1 has marked every pair separated by a string of length at most k−1, then pass k marks a pair separated by a first symbol a followed by such a string. When a pass adds nothing, no finite string can separate any remaining pair. Some syllabi describe the inner test as distinguishing one string from another.

Build the quotient DFA from the classes. The start state is [q0], the class containing q0. For a class [p] and symbol a, set δ'([p], a) = [δ(p, a)]. This is well defined: if p ≡ q, then δ(p, a) ≡ δ(q, a), otherwise a would distinguish p and q. A class is final if it contains a final state. All states in a class agree on finality.

Let Q_min be the set of classes. The quotient has |Q_min| states, and it accepts the same language as M. It has no pair of equivalent states, so it is minimal. Any minimal DFA for the same language is isomorphic to it: same state count, same transitions after renaming states. This is the uniqueness statement. The classes are exactly the right-invariant equivalence classes of the Myhill-Nerode relation: two strings x and y are equivalent when no continuation z makes xz accepted and yz rejected. The full theorem and proof are in Unit 2; here you only need the algorithm and the merge.

figure.caption: Pass 0 marks every final/non-final pair; pass 1 marks q1q2, because on a it reaches the marked q0q2; pass 2 marks nothing. q0q3 is never marked, so q0 and q3 merge, leaving a 3-state DFA that counts a’s mod 3.

examples.question: Minimise M = ({q0,q1,q2,q3}, {a,b}, δ, q0, {q0,q3}) with δ(q0,a)=q1, δ(q0,b)=q3; δ(q1,a)=q2, δ(q1,b)=q1; δ(q2,a)=q0, δ(q2,b)=q2; δ(q3,a)=q1, δ(q3,b)=q3. Show every pass of table filling and give the quotient DFA.
steps: Reachability: q0 is the start state; q1 = δ(q0,a), q2 = δ(q1,a), q3 = δ(q0,b). All four states are reachable, so none is deleted.
List the unordered pairs once: q0q1, q0q2, q0q3, q1q2, q1q3, q2q3.
Pass 0: F = {q0,q3}. Mixed pairs are marked: q0q1, q0q2, q1q3, q2q3. The pairs q0q3 and q1q2 stay unmarked because both states in each pair are both final or both non-final.

Pass 1: check q0q3. On a it goes to q1,q1; on b it goes to q3,q3. No marked pair is reached, so q0q3 stays unmarked. Check q1q2. On a it goes to q2,q0; the pair q0q2 is already marked, so q1q2 is marked. Pass 1 adds q1q2.
Pass 2: only q0q3 is unmarked. It again goes to equal states q1,q1 on a and q3,q3 on b. Nothing new is marked. Stop.
Classes: A = {q0,q3}, B = {q1}, C = {q2}. Quotient transitions: A on a → B, A on b → A; B on a → C, B on b → B; C on a → A, C on b → C. Start state is A; final state is A.
examples.answer: The minimal DFA has 3 states: A={q0,q3} (start and final), B={q1}, C={q2}; it accepts exactly strings whose number of a's is divisible by 3.

traps: Delete unreachable states first. A final state that no input can reach would otherwise survive as an extra class and inflate the minimal DFA.
Do not stop after pass 0 or after one loop. Run until a complete pass marks nothing new; otherwise some equivalent-looking pairs stay wrongly merged.
Two states that are both final, or both non-final, can still be distinguishable. Finality is only the length-0 test; later symbols can separate them.
Always treat δ(p,a) and δ(q,a) as an unordered pair when checking marks. The pair q2q0 is the same as q0q2, and order must not hide a mark.
A merge is valid only when every symbol keeps the pair inside one class. If δ(p,a) and δ(q,a) fall in different classes, p and q were distinguishable and must not be merged.

quiz.a: States p and q are distinguishable if some string w ∈ Σ* sends exactly one of δ̂(p,w) and δ̂(q,w) into F.

quiz.q: Why does the table-filling algorithm delete unreachable states before starting?
quiz.a: Unreachable states cannot affect the accepted language. If left in Q, they may form extra equivalence classes, so the quotient would not be the minimal DFA.

quiz.q: In the worked example, which pair is marked in pass 1 and why?
quiz.a: Pair q1q2 is marked. On symbol a it goes to q2,q0, and the pair q0q2 was already marked in pass 0. So a distinguishes q1 and q2.

quiz.q: Explain how two final states can still be distinguishable even though the empty string does not separate them.
quiz.a: Finality only tests length 0. A later string can lead one state to a final state and the other to a non-final state; that string is then a distinguishing string.

quiz.q: After the algorithm stops, you have unmarked pairs (p,q) and (q,r). How do you build the classes?
quiz.a: Take the transitive closure of the unmarked-pair relation. All states connected by unmarked pairs form one class; in this case p, q and r merge.

quiz.q: What does one pass of the repeat loop test?
quiz.a: It tests whether some symbol a takes an unmarked pair to an already marked pair. If so, the original pair is distinguishable by a longer string.

quiz.q: Why is the minimal DFA unique up to renaming of states?
quiz.a: The equivalence classes are fixed by the language: two states merge exactly when no continuation separates them. Any minimal DFA must have one state per class, so state count and transitions match after renaming.

beyond: Not for the exam. Hopcroft's algorithm minimizes a DFA faster by splitting classes with a worklist, and Moore's algorithm is another table-based variant. Lexer generators and regular-expression engines use DFA minimization to shrink transition tables before generating code. The same equivalence idea appears in model checking, where equivalent states of a protocol are collapsed. Search for Hopcroft DFA minimization, Moore's algorithm, and Myhill-Nerode equivalence classes.
